newsitem.title: USA: Fifth strep death cited in New York state.
newsitem.headline: Fifth strep death cited in New York state.

text.p: Medical authorities in Rochester, where a woman died last week of a rare "flesh-eating" bacteria, announced Wednesday the death of a fifth person from the strep infection that can cause the disease.

The five people died of invasive group A streptococcus, health officials in Monroe County, New York, said. But of the 19 people in the county infected so far this year with the Group A strep, only two contracted necrotizing fascitis, the so-called flesh-eating form, they said.
One died on Friday, and the other is recovering. Details of the most recent death were not immediately available.
Two deaths from Group A strep reported by officials late on Tuesday were women, one of whom died in January and the other in February, officials said. Their names were not released.
They had been patients at Strong Memorial Hospital in Rochester, where 39-year-old Susan Dougherty died of necrotizing fascitis on Friday.
Dougherty had a baby by Caesarean section at the hospital in February, and the bacteria started in her surgical wound, sources said.

"We have every reason to believe that the cluster of three cases among obstetrical patients is over and that it is entirely safe for patients to deliver babies or have surgery or whatever treatment they seek here at Strong Memorial," Paul Gramm, an infectious disease specialist at the hospital, said.

In nearby Ontario County, a rural area outside Rochester, a 10-year-old boy died from pneumonia associated with the Group A streptococcus, but he did not have the so-called flesh-eating bacteria, authorities said.

There are 10,000 to 15,000 cases of invasive Group A strep annually in the United States, the federal Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) in Atlanta, says. About one in 10 progresses to necrotizing fascitis, and death rates from this strain range from 20 percent to 60 percent, the CDC says.
